It defines the meaning and structure of web content. Other technologies besides HTML are generally used to describe a web page's appearance/presentation ( CSS ) or functionality/behavior ( JavaScript ). "Hypertext" refers to text containing links that connect web pages to one another, either within a single website or between websites. Links are a fundamental aspect of the Web. By uploading content to the Internet and linking it to pages created by other people, you become an active participant in the World Wide Web. HTML uses "markup" to annotate text, images, and other content for display in a Web browser. HTML markup includes special "elements" such as , , <body> , <header> , <footer> , <article> , <section> , <p> , <div> , <span> , <img> , <aside> , <audio> , <canvas> , <datalist> , <details> , <embed> , <nav> , <search> , <output> , <progress> , <video> , <ul> , <ol> , <li> and many others. An HTML element is set off from other text in a document by "tags", which consist of the element name surrounded by < and > . The name of an element inside a tag is case-insensitive. That is, it can be written in uppercase, lowercase, or a mixture. For example, the <title> tag can be written as <Title> , <TITLE> , or in any other way. pages.text: Huisdieren - Rijksmuseum Onderwerp Huisdieren Door de geschiedenis heen verandert de rol van huisdieren flink, van nuttige werkdieren tot geliefde metgezellen. Pas tussen 500 en 1500 beginnen edellieden honden te houden voor hun gezelschap. Lees meer Op schilderijen uit de 17de eeuw verschijnen deze viervoeters vaak in die rol. Katten worden lange tijd vooral ingezet als muizenverdelgers en hebben door de middeleeuwse associatie met hekserij een slechte reputatie. Pas in de Victoriaanse tijd accepteren mensen katten als huisdier. Een mooie raskat, zoals een Britse korthaar of de Perzische Langhaar, wordt een statussymbool voor rijke burgers. Vanaf de 19de eeuw worden honden en katten, en later vogels en vissen, alledaagse huisdieren voor alle lagen van de bevolking. Kunstenares Henriëtte Ronner-Knip (1821-1909) specialiseert zich in het schilderen van katten, wat haar bekendheid oplevert. Ze krijgt regelmatig de opdracht om de geliefde huisdieren van adellijke en burgerlijke families te vereeuwigen. But after four years in the UK, the draw of home has proven too strong and they have returned to Ukraine's third largest city, undeterred by the sustained threat of air raids. "Friends of ours thought we were idiots for going back to Ukraine," reflects John, 74. "But returning is something we felt we needed to do. "Yes, it's dangerous. Yes, there are drones flying overhead. Yes, you can hear the explosions. But you just have to get on with life as best you can. "Home is Ukraine." During their time away, the pair sought sanctuary in Hull , East Yorkshire, where John was born and raised and has a property. He met Liliya, 64, in Ukraine and had been living there for 30 years until the invasion. "We had built a good life here," he says. pages.text: Human Capital in Venture Capital: Evidence From 100,000 Venture Capitalists | NBER Skip to main content Human Capital in Venture Capital: Evidence From 100,000 Venture Capitalists Blake Jackson & Ilya A. Strebulaev Share X LinkedIn Facebook Bluesky Threads Email Link Working Paper 35501 DOI 10.3386/w35501 Issue Date July 2026 We study human capital in venture capital (VC) using a new dataset covering over 100,000 professionals affiliated with U.S. VC firms. Investment success is extremely concentrated: fewer than 40% of VCs with any investments are ever credited with a successful investment, and 90% of investment profits are generated by 5% of VCs. Differences in education, prior work experience, and demographics predict career progression and investment outcomes, consistent with persistent investor-specific skills. Quasi-experimental variation from marginal inclusions on the Forbes Midas List shows that achieving superstar status increases access to highly-valued startups, complementing other human capital and contributing to concentration. pages.text: Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient | National Geographic SCIENCE NOT EXACTLY ROCKET SCIENCE Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient By Ed Yong Published June 22, 2010 • 4 min read Stephen Wroe has built a career out of analysing some of the planet’s most formidable skulls. His group at the University of New South Wales have studied the strength, sturdiness and biting power of the sabre-toothed cat , the great white shark , and the Komodo dragon . Now, he has turned his attention to a predator whose skull is far less impressive but yields surprises all the same – us. Humans, it is said, have relatively weak jaws that can’t inflict or withstand high bite forces. Some have suggested that we are adapted to eat foods that aren’t very tough, or that our use of tools and cooking has lessened the evolutionary pressure on maintaining sturdy jaws. Some have even suggested that our weedy jaw muscles made way for our large brains and thus facilitated their evolution. But according to Wroe, all of these explanations have a fatal flaw – our jaws aren’t weak at all. They’re actually remarkably efficient for a primate. The notion of weak human chops was based on very unrefined models that treated our jaws as two-dimensional levers. Of course, in real life, we chew in three glorious dimensions. To really understand how strong our mandibles are, we need to add that third dimension to the models. That’s exactly what Wroe did. He used his signature technique, called finite element analysis , to create a virtual model of a human skull (belonging to a San hunter-gatherer).

pages.text: Human Subjects Protection and Institutional Review Board (IRB) | NBER Skip to main content Human Subjects Protection and Institutional Review Board (IRB) Share X LinkedIn Facebook Bluesky Threads Email Link The NBER and our funders are committed to protecting the rights, welfare and privacy of human subjects. Federal mandate (The Common Rule, 45 CFR pt. 46) and longstanding NBER policy require that the NBER IRB review and approve ALL research involving human subjects that is performed under the auspices of the NBER. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and 15 other federal agencies issued a final rule to update regulations that safeguard individuals who participate in research. Most provisions in the new rule were effective January 21, 2019. The new rule strengthens protections for people who volunteer to participate in research, while ensuring that the oversight system does not add inappropriate administrative burdens, particularly to low-risk research. It also allows more flexibility in keeping with today's dynamic research environment. Some categories of research are exempted from review by federal regulation. However, it is the NBER IRB’s responsibility to make a determination on a study’s exempt status, and so ALL projects involving human subjects at the NBER must be reviewed and either approved or ruled exempt by NBER IRB. The NBER IRB approval must be obtained BEFORE any human subjects studies are begun. pages.text: Humanitarian forensics | ICRC Skip to main content Humanitarian forensics: Applying forensic science for humanitarian purposes We ensure that universally recognized forensic standards are applied for the treatment and identification of the deceased, the search for missing people, and in any other situation where forensic science would address an issue of humanitarian concern. The principles that guide our work Forensic science for humanitarian action What the law says Latest articles Next event The principles that guide our work As a result of armed conflict, other situations of violence and natural disasters, people can get separated from their families, go missing or die. They may also become victims of ill-treatment and sexual violence, especially in the context of detention, displacement and migration. Medicolegal systems and forensic institutions play an essential role in addressing these issues of humanitarian concern. Humanitarian forensic action is the application of forensic science and investigative principles to humanitarian work. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) is the only organization to use forensic science for exclusively humanitarian purposes. pages.description: New research explores how diet, evolution, and facial anatomy may have shaped our modern smiles.
pages.text: Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? | National Geographic HEALTH Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? New research explores how diet, evolution, and facial anatomy may have shaped our modern smiles. Studies of ancient skulls show wider jaws and fewer malocclusions, leading researchers to explore how diet and lifestyle shaped the human face. Photograph by Alan/Adobe Stock By Leah Worthington Published July 15, 2025 Braces, rubber bands, even jaw surgery—millions endure them in pursuit of a straighter smile. But were misaligned smiles always this common? Research suggests that might not be the case. While malocclusions—crowded or misaligned teeth—have been found among our hunter-gatherer ancestors, they appear to be more prevalent in modern populations. So what changed? Experts say the answer isn’t simple but point to one possible culprit: our diets. As we traded raw, tough foods for softer, more processed ones, the burden of chewing decreased, allowing our jaws to shrink over time. Now, researchers are exploring how evolutionary biology, diet, and modern lifestyles may have reshaped our faces—and our smiles. How farming may have reshaped the human face Ancient human skulls were strikingly different from our own. Early hunter-gatherers had large, powerful jaws built for the demanding work of chewing tough meats, fibrous vegetables, seeds, and nuts. But around 12,000 years ago, things began to change. pages.text: Hundreds still homeless after 'unsafe' Canning Town flats evacuation Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Hundreds still homeless after being evacuated from 'unsafe' flats 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ayshea Buksh London BBC The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works, was advertised as "an exciting regeneration project" when it was built Hundreds of residents in east London remain homeless after structural defects were discovered at an award-winning high-rise development that was declared "at risk of sudden collapse". The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works in Canning Town, Newham, was built less than 10 years ago. But last month, people living there were suddenly told to leave - some in the middle of the night by London Fire Brigade - because it was "unsafe". Businesses renting commercial spaces were also told to evacuate their premises. Engineers identified concerns with reinforced concrete "transfer slabs" supporting the buildings - an issue that has emerged at other London developments, prompting wider scrutiny of the construction method. Property company Galliard Homes, which built the scheme, says it is working to "investigate the concerns and develop potential solutions", while giving financial and practical support to residents. pages.title: Hungary v Northern Ireland: We want to play on the biggest stages - Isaac Price - BBC Sport
pages.description: Before Tuesday's crucial trip to Hungary in the Nations League, midfielder Isaac Price says Northern Ireland want to play on the biggest stages.
pages.text: Hungary v Northern Ireland: We want to play on the biggest stages - Isaac Price - BBC Sport Image source, Press Eye Image caption, West Brom midfielder Isaac Price has started Northern Ireland's last 25 matches By Andy Gray BBC Sport NI Journalist Published 16 November 2026 When Northern Ireland step out into the Puskas Arena on Tuesday night, they hope it will be a taste of what is to come. In the 70,000-seater stadium, which hosted the Champions League final between Paris St-Germain and Arsenal in May, Northern Ireland's destiny will be in their own hands. In 18 months' time, Michael O'Neill's young side will hope be at the Euro 2028 finals. But for now, they face Hungary with hopes of promotion to League A in the Nations League for the first time. A win or a draw will do the job in Budapest, and it would be the latest step for a Northern Ireland side who continue to show encouraging signs in their development. Worst case, NI will still have a shot at a play-off for League A in March but their sole aim is to get the job done on Tuesday. Midfielder Isaac Price, who has grown into a key player under O'Neill, says you "have got to love the expectation". "That's what you play football for. We're playing in a stadium where 70,000 people will be watching and then there'll be loads more at home watching," he told BBC Sport NI. "That's what you grow up and want to do. You've got to play on the biggest stages and that's what it'll be tomorrow [Tuesday] night."
